# 10 — Master Evidence Log

Every substantive claim made anywhere in this audit traces back to a row in this table. Observations are quoted verbatim wherever the source was text; where the source was a runtime measurement, the exact numeric value is given.

**Collection window:** 2026-08-14. **Target:** `https://web.telegram.org/a/`, app version `12.0.38`, deployment built `2026-08-11 15:24:14 UTC`.

**Three collection channels, each with different trust properties:**

| Channel | What it produced | Trust note |
|---|---|---|
| **Passive asset fetch** (`curl`/HTTP over the container's egress proxy) | 461 JS, 25 CSS, 4 WASM, 6 workers, 453 source maps, all response headers | Headers and bodies unaffected by the proxy; the proxy does not rewrite content. TLS chain read separately through a raw `CONNECT` tunnel. |
| **Live authenticated session** (Playwright, headless Chromium, desktop 1600×1000 @2× DPR, UA spoofed to Chrome 140/macOS, real account `+370 632 65395`) | DOM, storage, WebSocket frames, layout geometry, console, settings copy, 72 delivered screenshots | Egress proxy rejected Chromium's TLS ClientHello, so a TLS-terminating relay was inserted and `--disable-http2` was set. **Structural findings unaffected; all latency numbers are not production-representative.** |
| **Public source repo** (`git clone --depth 1 Ajaxy/telegram-tt`, HEAD `d915b1b9ae856eb9eae737d1816d9c05df66b1d3`) | Source-level confirmation of runtime observations | Repo `version` is `12.0.38`, matching the deployment exactly, so source and deployment are the same build generation. |

Confidence values: **Confirmed** / **Strong inference** / **Possible** / **Unknown**.

**A note on length.** This log runs to **186 rows**, above the 60–100 originally scoped. That is deliberate: it is the single evidence base for nine documents, and every row is cited by at least one of them. Sections are independently readable — A–C cover identity and delivery, D–G the build and dependency graph, H–I the live protocol and storage behaviour, J–L the measured UI, M–N defects and performance, O licensing. If a shorter version is wanted, sections D, F and L compress well; J (per-breakpoint geometry) and N (performance, with its caveats) do not.

| # | Area | Source | Observation (verbatim) | Interpretation | Confidence |

| 15 | Headers | `GET /a/assets/index-IZ97MA_m.js` | `cache-control: max-age=3600` / `expires: Fri, 14 Aug 2026 13:39:38 GMT` / `x-served-by: meta4240619` | **Content-hashed immutable asset gets the same 1-hour TTL as the HTML.** No `immutable`, no `max-age=31536000`. | 16 | Load balancing | Repeated requests | `x-served-by:` `meta4240719`, `meta4240822`, `meta4240420`, `meta4240118`, … | Rotates per request → round-robin across a self-hosted node pool (`meta424xxxx` naming), not a commercial CDN edge. | Confirmed |
| 17 | Compression | `Accept-Encoding: br` on a JS asset | served **identity**, 28,951 bytes | Brotli is not supported by the origin. | Confirmed |
| 18 | Compression | `Accept-Encoding: br, gzip, deflate, zstd` | `content-encoding: gzip` | gzip only. No Brotli, no zstd. Explicitly probed, not assumed. | Confirmed |
| 19 | Protocol | Response header set, all requests | `alt-svc` **absent** | HTTP/3 is not advertised. Negotiated protocol is HTTP/2. | Confirmed |
| 20 | Transport security | Response header set, all requests | `strict-transport-security` **absent** | **No HSTS header on any observed response.** | Confirmed |
| 21 | CSP | Response header set vs `index.html` | No `content-security-policy` header; CSP present as `<meta http-equiv>` | CSP is delivered in the document, generated by `vite.config.ts` into both dev headers and prod HTML. | Confirmed |

Read through a raw tunnel so this is the origin's real chain, not the audit proxy's. | Confirmed |

| 30 | SSR | `index.html`, 5,806 B raw | No inlined state, no server-rendered markup, no critical-CSS inlining | Fully static app shell. **No SSR.** | Confirmed |

Headings: **1** correct `<h1>`. `<html lang>`: `"en"`. `<title>`: `"Telegram"` (generic). | Fundamentals right, visual/structural accessibility weak. | Confirmed |
| 178 | Accessibility | Manual, computed styles + pixel diff | Both CTAs are real `<button type="button" class="Button auth-button default primary text">`; **0** `[role="button"]` divs; **0** elements with `tabindex`; tab order is exactly 2 elements in DOM order, no traps. **But on focus:** `outline: none`, `box-shadow: none`, `border: 0px none` — the only affordance is `background-color: rgba(74,149,214,0.08)`, i.e. `#F0F7FC` over `#ffffff` ≈ **1.08:1 contrast** | **WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11 requires 3:1 for focus indicators.** At 1.08:1 the indicator is effectively invisible. axe did **not** flag this (it does not evaluate `:focus-visible` appearance) — an additional finding beyond the 4 automated violations. There are **zero `:focus`/`:focus-visible` rules matching these buttons** across all `document.styleSheets`. | Confirmed |

**Caveats that apply to every row in section N:** all timing was collected in a container whose egress proxy rejected Chromium's TLS ClientHello, so a TLS-terminating relay was inserted and `--disable-http2` was set. Every resource reports `nextHopProtocol = "http/1.1"`; the real site is HTTP/2. MTProto WebSockets failed through the proxy (`code 1006`), and the app fell back to a slower transport. Heap figures are 100 KB-quantized. Request counts, byte counts, storage inventory, cache-hit behaviour, accessibility findings and responsive breakpoints were **byte-identical across all runs** and are trustworthy regardless of environment; latency figures are not.

## Claims we deliberately did NOT make, and why

A sloppier audit would have asserted each of the following. We did not, and the reason matters more than the claim.

**1. Production latency figures.** Every timing number in section N was collected over **HTTP/1.1 through a TLS-terminating Python relay from a US-egress datacenter IP**, in headless Chromium with no GPU. We report FCP 2,536 ms and time-to-CTA 8,854 ms *as measured in that environment*, tagged as such, and we refuse to present them as what a real user experiences. We also refuse the tempting inverse — we do not claim the app is "actually fast in production," because we did not measure that either. What survives the environment is: request counts, byte counts, the loaded-vs-available split, cache-hit behaviour, storage inventory, breakpoints, and DOM node counts, all of which were byte-identical across runs.

**2. "Fast 3G" as a 3G estimate.** The CDP throttle was measured to be **largely non-binding** (baseline aggregate throughput 0.45 Mbps against a 1.6 Mbps cap). Reporting "+11 % FCP on Fast 3G" as a mobile-network finding would be actively misleading. Only the 4× CPU row is quoted as a real result, because CPU throttling is unaffected by the network path.

**3. Screen-reader behaviour.** We ran axe-core and did manual keyboard, focus-ring, landmark and tab-order checks. We did **not** test with NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver or Orca. So we state that `aria-label="AccDescrPollVoteDown"` will be *announced as that string* (a mechanical consequence of the DOM), and that the app keeps inactive screens mounted so the accessibility tree is ambiguous — but we make **no claim about actual usability with assistive technology**, in either direction. The open upstream issue "Improve screen reader accessibility" (filed 2022-04-05, still open, unassigned, no label or milestone) is reported as a fact about the issue tracker, not as a verdict on the app.

**4. Anything about Telegram's server-side implementation.** We observed six `zws*.web.telegram.org` WebSocket endpoints, a rotating `x-served-by: meta424xxxx` header, and AS62041 hosting. We do **not** claim to know the DC topology, how many nodes are in the pool, how sessions are routed or load-balanced, what the server does with an `upload.getFile`, or how push notifications are dispatched. Every server-side statement here is an inference *about the client's model of the server*, drawn from client code.

**5. The "Jolly Cobra" / "Ace Monkey" codename mapping.** Telegram never published which contest codename belongs to which developer. The Jolly Cobra → `Ajaxy` mapping rests on the telegram-tt README's own first-prize claim for `contest.com/javascript-web-3` matching the contest channel's 1st-place award; Ace Monkey → `morethanwords` is weaker still. **Flagged as inference, not fact**, wherever the contest history is discussed.

**6. "Telegram Air" as a product.** Releases are tagged `air_v2.10.3`, the Teact README references "Telegram Air (Web A)", and a mirror carries `Telegram.Air-aarch64.dmg`. But `telegram.org/apps` lists no such product and `web.telegram.org/a/get` is titled "Telegram A Desktop". Best supported statement: **"Telegram Air" is the internal/release name for packaged Tauri desktop builds; its status as a publicly branded product is unconfirmed.**

**7. Any "60fps philosophy."** We found **no Telegram statement using "60fps"** as a stated target for the web clients. The only first-party frame-rate reference we could source is a *Web K* contest brief mentioning "noticeable lagging on devices with **120 FPS displays**" — a different client, and a defect description rather than a principle. We do not attribute a frame-rate doctrine to Telegram. What we *do* assert, because it is in the code, is that the update pass defers on `getIsBlockingAnimating()`, that `beginHeavyAnimation()` gates state updates and IDB writes, and that ten animations are individually user-toggleable.

**8. A "we benchmarked React and it was too slow" origin story for Teact.** The only documented cause is a contest rule banning third-party UI frameworks. There is no interview, talk, HN comment or blog post from the author explaining "why not React" — we searched. A Teact-vs-React-18-vs-Preact-10 benchmark exists but publishes **no numbers** and postdates the framework by two years, so it is validation, not justification. Any narrative that inverts this sequence is unsupported by the record.

**9. A "no published design principles" claim dressed up as one.** There is **no first-party Telegram design-principles document** for its own clients. What exists is a *judging rubric* — "our main criteria for evaluation will be speed, size of the apps and attention to detail", plus a $500 bonus explicitly for bundle-size progress and $500–$1,000 penalties for broken 2FA and cross-browser breakage. We quote that as the rubric the client was built to satisfy, and we do not upgrade it into a philosophy statement Telegram never made.

**10. Bundle-size before/after against the 2021 "400 KB" claim.** Telegram's launch post claimed the web apps need "only a 400 KB download". Our measurement is ~305 KiB gzip for the statically-enumerated eager path (or ~307 KiB by a slightly different runtime enumeration, or 683,895 B transferred for all 48 login-screen subresources). **The blog never defines what it measured**, so these cannot be presented as a before/after and we do not.

**11. A verdict on production error rates.** Zero application-level JS exceptions across our authenticated walkthrough and all six cold runs is a real observation, but it covers one account, one session, a handful of screens and roughly an hour. It is evidence that the happy paths we exercised are clean. It is **not** evidence of a low production error rate — and note that with no telemetry in the bundle (rows 85–86), neither we nor Telegram would learn about most client-side failures from the client itself.

**12. Legal conclusions.** The GPLv3 analysis in this audit is engineering reading of a license text, flagged as inference throughout. "Internal use does not trigger conveying" and "serving GPL'd JS to a third-party browser is a grey zone" are how practitioners generally treat it — **not legal advice, and explicitly to be confirmed with counsel** before any code from this repo influences taskrgram beyond the level of ideas.
